caption:
Was the Feejee mermaid real? No. It was a monkey's head and torso sewn to the back half of a fish.

A captain named Samuel Barrett Edes bought it from Japanese sailors in 1822 for $6,000 — money taken from his ship's expense account. Another account says an American whaler's captain paid $5,000 in Batavia.

The objects were made commercially in Japan. A Dutch warehouse keeper on Dejima, J. F. van Overmeer Fisscher, recorded that one cost 30 ryō, about 60 guilders, and could be sold in Batavia for 2,000 Spanish dollars. Sellers also offered him two-headed men, face-on-belly figures and twin-headed dragons.

It was shown in London in 1822 at the Turf Coffee-house, St James's Street. Edes' son sold it to Moses Kimball of the Boston Museum in 1842. Kimball kept ownership; P. T. Barnum leased it for $12.50 a week. Barnum's naturalist would not attest to it. Barnum ran it anyway, planting anonymous letters in New York papers about a "Dr. J. Griffin" — actually his associate Levi Lyman — and printing 10,000 pamphlets.

Barnum described it himself: "an ugly, dried-up, black-looking, diminutive specimen, about 3 feet long."

What is unresolved: the original disappeared, likely burned in one of the fires that destroyed parts of Barnum's collections. Ripley's, Coney Island's Sideshow by the Seashore and Bobby Reynolds' sideshow all claim to hold the true original. Joe Nickell calls them "fakes of Barnum's fake."

Images: George Cruikshank's 1822 etching; a papier-mâché mermaid from the Kimball collection at the Peabody Museum, photographed by Daderot; the Banff Merman photographed by Eviatar Bach; Mōri Baien's 1825 painting; an illustration from Barnum's 1855 autobiography; and a page from Henry Lee's Sea Fables Explained, 1883.
